# Diagnosing Heat-Related Ignition Failures in the Ford Figo

When a 2013 Ford Figo refuses to crank specifically after sitting in direct sunlight, the issue almost certainly lies within the engine's thermal management or starting system rather than a generic "bad starter" scenario. The fact that the vehicle starts reliably in the morning or during cooler conditions rules out a simple dead battery or a mechanically seized motor. Instead, you are dealing with a classic thermal expansion problem where components hit their operating limits before the ignition sequence can complete.

The most probable culprit in this specific configuration is the Idle Air Control Valve (IACV) or the Throttle Body acting up due to heat soak. In many Figo models from that era, these components use plastic actuators and internal seals that degrade over time. When parked under intense solar radiation, the engine block radiates heat into the intake manifold and valve cover. If the IACV pintle gets stuck or the throttle body flap seizes due to thermal expansion of the housing, the Engine Control Unit (ECU) cannot establish the necessary idle speed to initiate a start. The ECU expects a specific voltage feedback from these sensors; if they are physically restricted by heat, the engine management system may cut fuel injection or ignition timing as a fail-safe, resulting in no crank or a single click.

Another critical failure point is the fuel pump relay or the primary fuel pump itself. Fuel pumps generate significant heat during operation, but when the car sits in the sun, the surrounding air temperature can approach the boiling point of gasoline if ventilation is poor. More importantly, the electrical resistance in the wiring harness for the fuel pump increases with temperature. If the harness is routed near hot exhaust components or under a sun-heated hood, the voltage drop across the relay contacts might exceed the threshold required to energize the pump coil. This creates a scenario where the pump works fine when cold but fails to pull enough current to spin the diaphragm once ambient temperatures rise.

To verify this without immediately replacing expensive parts like the fuel pump assembly, you can perform a voltage drop test across the fuel pump relay connector while the engine is hot and attempting to start. If you measure less than 12V at the input side of the relay but the key is turned, the issue is likely upstream in the power distribution or the ECU's ground reference. Conversely, if voltage is present but the pump doesn't click, the coil resistance has likely increased beyond its specification due to heat.

A common pitfall for owners visiting dealerships repeatedly is that technicians often replace the starter motor without addressing the root cause of the thermal seizure. Since the starter only engages once the crankshaft position sensor confirms movement (which requires fuel and spark), a thermal failure in the fuel system or intake control will mimic a bad starter symptom. The recurring nature of the problem after "fixes" suggests that the thermal expansion coefficient of the original plastic components hasn't been addressed, simply swapped with another unit destined for the same fate.

If you are attempting to resolve this programmatically via ECU tuning (which is advanced and carries warranty risks), one might consider modifying the fuel cut-off threshold in the cold-start map to compensate for the reduced pump efficiency at high temperatures. However, hardware integrity checks should always precede software interventions. Ensure the wiring harness is insulated and routed away from heat sources before assuming an electronic fault.
